newsitem.title: PANAMA: Panama economy to grow 3.5 pct in 1997, official.
newsitem.headline: Panama economy to grow 3.5 pct in 1997, official.

text.p: Panama's economy is projected to grow 3.5 percent in 1997, up from 2.5 percent last year, a top government official said Wednesday.
"We expect Panama's economy to grow 3.5 percent this year," Planning and Economic Policy Minister Guillermo Chapman told the Foreign Press Association.
"We see growth in many sectors," he said without providing details. "Our estimations are more conservative than the World Bank which predicts 4.0 percent growth," he added.

In 1996, Panama's GDP grew to about $8.5 billion from $8.2 billion in 1995, the first time the small central American nation registered major growth since the early part of the decade in the wake of the December 1989 U.S. invasion, he said.
Panama's economic growth reached an all-time high of 9.4 percent in 1991, but growth slowed in subsequent years.
Some local economic analysts said investors believed a 1997 growth rate of 2.5 percent was more realistic.

"Last year the government set projections higher and they weren't accomplished," said one analyst, who requested anonymity. "They didn't foresee that the pillars of our economy -- the free zone, banana and construction sectors -- would show a decrease."
"We would need at least six percent growth to bring down unemployment and other serious problems we face in order to root out poverty," he said.
Chapman acknowledged the fight against two of Panama's biggest problems -- unemployment and poverty -- had been the most challenging for the administration of President Ernesto Perez Balladares.
He reiterated that Panama's unemployment rate stood at 13.9 percent at the end of 1996, compared with 14 percent a year earlier. He gave no fresh figures.
About two-fifths of the nation's 2.5 million inhabitants live in extreme poverty, or about 30 percent, down from 45 percent in 1990, he said.

"The biggest problems of the country are poverty and the distribution of wealth. It's something we cannot solve overnight," he said. "We're trying to reduce tariffs and ensure more competition to alleviate Panama's high cost of living."

Perez Balladares, who took office in 1994, has pledged to help Panama's poor and open the country's traditionally-closed economy to trade by reducing tariffs, privatizing state enterprises and strengthening banking laws.
